title: How do you implement soft delete in Hibernate using @SQLDelete, @Where/@SQLRestriction, @Filter, and the newer @SoftDelete? What are the trade-offs?
shortTitle: How do you implement soft delete?
keyPoints: Soft delete marks a row as deleted instead of physically removing it, preserving history and allowing recovery.
@SQLDelete rewrites the entity's DELETE into an UPDATE that sets the deleted flag.
@SQLRestriction (Hibernate 6+) adds a static WHERE deleted=false to every query, auto-filtering deleted rows.
@Filter defines a dynamic, parameterized filter that can be enabled or disabled per session for audit/admin views.
@SoftDelete (Hibernate 6.4+) is a single annotation that wires up the deleted column, rewrite, and filtering automatically.
Unique constraints become tricky because soft-deleted rows still occupy the table; use partial indexes or include the deleted flag.
Native queries bypass @SQLRestriction, so they can accidentally return deleted rows.

s1_definition.oneliner: Soft delete marks a row as deleted instead of removing it; `@SQLDelete` turns DELETE into UPDATE, `@SQLRestriction` auto-filters queries, `@Filter` is a dynamic toggle, and `@SoftDelete` does it all in one annotation.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Soft delete** -- never physically remove a row; mark it as deleted (boolean flag or timestamp) and filter it from normal queries.
- **@SQLDelete** -- rewrites the entity's DELETE into a custom SQL statement, typically `UPDATE ... SET deleted = true`.
- **@SQLRestriction** (Hibernate 6+) -- adds a static `WHERE deleted = false` to every SELECT for the entity, replacing the older `@Where`.
- **@Filter** -- a dynamic, parameterized filter you enable per session; useful for admin/audit views that need to include deleted rows.
- **@SoftDelete** (Hibernate 6.4+) -- a single annotation that manages the deleted column, rewrites deletes, and filters selects automatically.
- **Trade-offs** -- unique constraints, table bloat, native query bypass, and cascading soft deletes require careful handling.
s1_definition.analogy: When National Bank of India "closes" an account, it does not shred the file -- regulations require keeping records for years. Instead, Rajesh stamps it "CLOSED" and moves it to an archive drawer that is skipped during normal daily work. `@SQLDelete` is the rule that "delete" means "stamp as closed." `@SQLRestriction` is the standing instruction "ignore anything stamped closed." `@Filter` is a switch the auditor can flip to say "today, include closed files too." `@SoftDelete` is a single policy that sets up all of this automatically.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Soft Delete Annotation Stack:

  @SQLDelete + @SQLRestriction (manual):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  delete(entity)                           │
  │       │                                   │
  │       ▼                                   │
  │  @SQLDelete intercepts                    │
  │  UPDATE accounts SET deleted=true WHERE id=?│
  │                                           │
  │  findAll()                                │
  │       │                                   │
  │       ▼                                   │
  │  @SQLRestriction appends                  │
  │  WHERE deleted = false                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  @SoftDelete (automatic, Hibernate 6.4+):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @SoftDelete(columnName="deleted")        │
  │                                           │
  │  delete(entity) → UPDATE SET deleted=true │
  │  findAll()      → WHERE deleted=false     │
  │  Column managed automatically             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

```text
  @Filter (dynamic toggle):

  Normal user request:          Auditor request:
  filter enabled                filter NOT enabled
  (isDeleted=false)             (all rows visible)
       │                              │
       ▼                              ▼
  Active accounts only          All accounts
  (deleted rows hidden)         (deleted rows visible)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Soft delete means you never physically remove a row; you mark it as deleted with a flag or timestamp and filter it from normal queries. In Hibernate, `@SQLDelete` intercepts the delete and replaces it with an UPDATE that sets the flag, and `@SQLRestriction` appends a static `WHERE deleted = false` to every query so deleted rows are invisible. `@Filter` provides a dynamic toggle that auditors can enable to see deleted records. And `@SoftDelete` in Hibernate 6.4+ combines all of this into a single annotation.

The trade-offs are real. Unique constraints need partial indexes because soft-deleted rows still occupy the table. Native queries bypass `@SQLRestriction` and can accidentally return deleted rows. Table bloat accumulates without periodic archival. And cascading soft delete requires service-layer logic because JPA cascade only applies to physical operations.

At National Bank of India, a closed account was once hard-deleted and was unavailable for a regulatory audit. Rajesh moved to soft delete so the record is preserved. Day-to-day screens never see closed accounts thanks to `@SQLRestriction`, while the audit view uses `@Filter` to include them. A partial unique index on the email column ensures re-creating a soft-deleted account does not violate the uniqueness constraint.

Remember one sentence: soft delete marks rows as deleted instead of removing them, `@SQLDelete` + `@SQLRestriction` implement it manually, `@SoftDelete` does it in one annotation, and always handle unique constraints and native queries carefully.
